conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you so much for making time for this today. My name is Maya, and I’m one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I specialize in caring for new mothers and the emotional ups-and-downs that can show up after a baby arrives.

To get a quick snapshot of how you’re feeling, I’d like to run through a short screening questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s just 10 questions that ask about your mood, thoughts, and well-being over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting—think of it as a temperature check so we know how best to support you.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless there’s a safety concern, and you’re welcome to pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable. When you’re ready, we’ll go through each question together. I’ll re-phrase them conversationally so it feels more natural, and you can answer in your own words—no need for numbers or letters.

Do you have any questions before we start? If not, let’s dive in:

Over the past week, when you have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how has that felt for you—easy, sometimes, not often, or not at all?

Honestly, most of the time it feels like the joy has been sucked out of me. I can still crack a smile if someone tries really hard to be funny, but it’s rare and it fades fast. I used to laugh at little things—my husband’s dumb jokes, silly memes—but now it’s like I’m watching life through fogged glass. I *want* to feel light again, but mostly I just feel… flat, like the laugh gets stuck somewhere between my chest and my throat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes I can laugh, but it’s not the same—it feels forced or fades quickly. Most of the time I just don’t find things funny anymore, even when I know they should be.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like another chore. I wake up and think, “What’s the point?” I still do the basics for the baby, but anything extra feels overwhelming and joyless.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes—pretty much every day. If the baby’s fussy, I assume it’s because I’m not soothing him right. If I can’t breast-feed smoothly, I tell myself I’m failing him. Even little spills or bumps make me think, “A good mom would’ve prevented that.” I lie in bed replaying everything I did wrong, convincing myself he deserves better than me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

All the time. I’ll be sitting there, everything quiet, and suddenly my heart’s racing and my mind jumps to all the ways he could stop breathing or get sick. I check his chest rising like every two minutes. There doesn’t have to be a trigger—my body just flips into panic mode, and then I feel stupid afterward for getting so worked up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, that’s been happening a lot. Out of nowhere I’ll get this wave of fear—like something awful is about to happen, even when nothing’s going on. My chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and for a minute I feel like I’m losing control. It passes after a bit, but it leaves me shaky and embarrassed.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m drowning. It’s not that I can’t do the essentials—I feed him, change him, keep him safe—but everything feels ten times heavier. One dirty bottle in the sink can make me want to cry. When he won’t settle, I rock him and whisper “please, please,” because I’m scared I’ll never get a break. I manage, but I’m white-knuckling it, and by evening I’m exhausted and on edge.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down and my head just keeps spinning—did I sanitize the pump parts, is he breathing, am I already ruining him? Some nights I finally drift off, but then every squeak from the bassinet jerks me awake. I end up staring at the ceiling until the sky turns gray, and when he cries for his next feed I’m still wired and exhausted.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be holding the baby and suddenly feel tears coming—sometimes I end up crying while I’m feeding him. I try to tell myself it’s just hormones, but the sadness feels heavy and real, and it doesn’t lift like I keep hoping it will.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. I’ll be folding his tiny clothes or just staring out the window and the tears start rolling. Sometimes I can’t even name why—I just feel overwhelmed and hollow, and crying seems like the only release I have.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—no thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he needs.

You've described feeling as though joy has been drained from everyday moments, replaced by a persistent gray cloud of sadness and worry. Feeding, soothing, and simply getting through each task feel overwhelming, and even small chores can spark tears. You're keenly aware of how different things used to be-sharing laughs with your husband, looking forward to coffee with a friend-and you long to feel that lightness again. Despite this heavy load, you continue to meet your baby's basic needs, motivated by a deep desire to be the mom he deserves.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to enjoy humor, describes laughter as forced or fleeting, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory joy and sense of pointlessness, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily self-blame across multiple mothering tasks, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, unprovoked anxiety with physical panic symptoms and obsessive infant safety checking.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>The mother describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," equating her experience to "drowning" and stating tasks feel "ten times heavier," clearly aligning with the option of not being able to cope at all most of the time.</sym>, <sym>She describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep nearly every night due to persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, persistent sadness that interferes with routine care and feels heavy and unrelenting, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports tearfulness "a few times this week," matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 26/30 places you well above the 14-point cutoff that signals probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse core symptoms matching <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, recurrent anxiety and panic, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and tearfulness. High scores on items 3, 4, 5, and 6 highlight intense guilt, free-floating anxiety, panic-like episodes, and perceived inability to cope, all contributing to significant functional impairment. Denial of self-harm keeps safety risk lower, yet daily distress warrants immediate evaluation and support. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to review results and discuss treatment options
2. Request formal assessment using <med>PHQ-9</med> and <med>GAD-7</med> for diagnostic clarity and severity tracking
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, or <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
4. Plan daily 15-minute self-care windows (shower, short walk, quiet tea) and accept help with chores to reduce overload
5. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or guided imagery when <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise; keep a printed copy on the fridge for quick access
6. Arrange partner or family night shifts when possible to allow 4-hour blocks of uninterrupted sleep; discuss safe co-sleeping alternatives if needed
7. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress; emergency contact numbers for after-hours support
8. Store crisis text line and local emergency department info in your phone for any escalating distress or new thoughts of self-harm
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale–style questionnaire, patient self-report

Symptoms/observations  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (loss of pleasure/interest)  
- Daily guilt/self-blame (“failing as a mom”)  
- Anxiety symptoms: near-constant worry, nocturnal rumination, panic-like episodes (tight chest, breathlessness)  
- Functional overload: routine tasks perceived as “ten times heavier,” emotional exhaustion  
- Sleep disruption secondary to racing thoughts and hypervigilance re infant safety  
- Spontaneous crying, feels “hollow,” sadness present “pretty much every day”  
- Denies any self-harm ideation (explicit “No” to Q10)

Pattern  
Symptoms cluster consistently with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; onset post-delivery, intensity impairs coping but not meeting danger-to-self threshold at present.

Risk indicators  
- High: daily sadness, anhedonia, excessive guilt, panic symptoms  
- Moderate: sleep loss, perceived inability to cope  
- Low (present): absence of suicidal or infanticidal thoughts, protective desire to “feel better for baby”

Screening conclusion  
Elevated scores consistent with significant postpartum depression/anxiety; further clinical evaluation (diagnostic interview, PHQ-9, GAD-7), psychoeducation, and safety-planning recommended. No emergent safety issues identified at this time.
